title: Benjamin's Family and Saul's Line
overview: This chapter lists the families of the tribe of Benjamin, singling out those who lived in Jerusalem and tracing the family of King Saul for many generations.

parts.label: Benjamin's sons (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: This list of Benjamin's sons and grandsons does not fully match the ones in Genesis 46, Numbers 26 or chapter 7. The writer likely drew on different family records, and no one knows for sure how to fit them together.

parts.label: Ehud's family moved (vv. 6-7)
parts.note: These family heads from Geba, a town in Benjamin, were forced to move to Manahath, probably in Judah's territory. This Ehud may be the hero of Judges 3, who was also from Benjamin, but the Hebrew here is hard to follow and scholars are unsure who moved them and why.

parts.label: Shaharaim in Moab (vv. 8-13)
parts.note: A man named Shaharaim sent away two of his wives and had more sons while living in Moab, east of the Dead Sea; the text does not say why he was there. His grandsons built the towns of Ono and Lod and drove out the people of Gath, a Philistine city.

parts.label: Leading families in Jerusalem (vv. 14-28)
parts.note: These are the heads of Benjamin's main clans, and the list stresses that they lived in Jerusalem, which sat on Benjamin's border with Judah. Many think this mattered to families returning from exile in Babylon, who wanted to know where their ancestors had lived.

parts.label: Saul's family tree (vv. 29-34)
parts.note: This traces Saul, Israel's first king, back to a family based at Gibeon, a town near Jerusalem. His son Esh-Baal and grandson Merib-Baal appear in the books of Samuel as Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth, likely because later writers swapped 'Baal' (here probably just meaning 'lord') for a word meaning 'shame'.

parts.label: Jonathan's line continues (vv. 35-40)
parts.note: Jonathan's descendants are followed for more than ten generations, far longer than any other branch of Saul's family, possibly because of David's promise to be kind to Jonathan's family. The list ends with Ulam's sons, skilled archers whose clan grew to 150 men.

think: Is there value in knowing where your family came from, even when the record has gaps and some unflattering stories in it?
